extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and members/leaders of peer-group writing workshops
extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules and evaluative criteria for writing, revising, and critiquing fiction (description, action, focus, trajectory) plus explicit protocols for peer-group/online workshop practice and critique. Covers descriptive technique, revision exercises, story/plot definitions, and group critique etiquette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every detail must tell
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything you describe is there in order to further that story. Every detail must tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give us evidences that build up into a consistent, coherent mood or atmosphere from which we can infer the absent person or untold act. A mere inventory of articles won't do and will bore the reader. If using implication, you may repeat the exercise in a character's voice instead of the authorial voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use senses beyond sight
rubrics_metrics.description: In descriptive writing, give a thought from time to time to the senses other than sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sound is especially evocative. Mention of a certain scent or stink can set a feeling-tone. We have limited vocabulary for smell, so use it sparingly but purposefully. Taste and touch are forbidden to the detached author; the involved author may evoke how things feel to the hand, but should not have the narrator actually eat. If a character is telling the story, all senses may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication as technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell information by implication rather than by explicit exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break up invented or necessary exposition and slip it into conversation, action-narration, passing reference, or hint so readers don't realize they're learning background. Use implication to let readers understand without feeling 'lumpy' exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expository Lump — Fantastic Lump
rubrics_metrics.description: Take invented/fantastic background information and use it as the foundation of a scene or story, integrating it so it doesn't feel lumpy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the false history until familiar, then compost the information: break it up, spread it out, slip it into dialogue or action. Tell it by implication and include enough that readers can fully understand the situation. Aim for two or three pages (possibly more) for a scene that makes the invented information comprehensible without overt exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expository Lump — Real Lump
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a real complex process you know how to do and write a scene in which the process is happening, integrating necessary explanation into the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a process not everyone knows (bread-making, shoeing a horse, etc.). Keep the description specific and concrete, avoid unnecessary jargon (but use specialized lingo if it belongs), make the steps clear to the reader, and ensure the process doesn't become the entire piece—it should serve the scene or conversation and supply sensory details to keep it vivid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowding (density of detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowding: load the story with vivid, exact, concrete details and keep it full of what's happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid flabby language and clichés; prefer two exact words to ten vague ones. Keep the story moving, interconnected with echoes forward and backward. Use dense, rich sensory and meaningful detail to enrich the prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaping (selective omission)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaping: what you leap over (omit) matters — leave out non-relevant material and provide white space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listing is not describing. Only the relevant belongs. Over-including everything clogs the story. After crowding in the draft, leap boldly in revision by cutting padding, repetitions, or irrelevant material to reveal the story's shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft by crowding, revise by cutting
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactically, crowd in the first draft (put everything in), then in revision cut what merely pads, repeats, slows, or impedes the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide what counts and what tells; cut and recombine until what's left is what counts. Severe cutting intensifies style and forces both crowding and leaping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action writing: include only needed details
rubrics_metrics.description: In action sequences include what the reader needs to know and nothing more; avoid blow-by-blow accounts that create confusion and boredom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for transparent language, intense brief sensory details, and a clear sense of where we are and what's happening (Patrick O'Brian's sea battles are given as exemplary). Recognize inherent sameness in some action and make choices that enrich and speed the action rather than bog it down with every stroke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus (central subject) of a story
rubrics_metrics.description: A story needs a focus — what is it about? Who is it about? — explicit or implicit, around which all elements refer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The focus may be complex and hard to define, but it is the center to which events, characters, and passages contribute. Keep the narrative elements in service of that focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trajectory (shape/movement of story)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story needs a trajectory — a movement or shape that the narrative follows toward its end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trajectory is not necessarily an outline but a movement (straight, roundabout, recurrent, eccentric) that never ceases; every passage should contribute to this movement. Crowding and leaping should respect the trajectory (include what belongs to the focus and leap along the movement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Severe cutting (Exercise Ten)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a narrative over 400 words and cut it by half while keeping the narrative clear and the sensory impact vivid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires more than light pruning: count words and reduce to half, do not replace specifics with generalities, and avoid 'somehow.' If there is dialogue, cut any long speech or conversation in half implacably. The exercise trains discipline and helps identify Styrofoam versus heavy gold in your prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision heuristic: throw out early pages (Chekhov's advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rough rule in revision, consider removing early material—Chekhov suggested 'throw out the first three pages.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers often circle around and over-explain at the start; if the beginning can be cut, cut it. Also remove passages that stick out or leave the main trajectory and test whether the story joins up without them—often it does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the story tell itself (self-control)
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer should keep ego, opinions, and extraneous mental clutter out of the way to find the story's focus and follow its movement; the story is the end and the writer is the means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being ready to let a story tell itself requires craft skills and readiness to guide it where it ought to go. The discipline of art is freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-group workshop — optimal size and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: A peer-group workshop works best with about six or seven up to ten or eleven members; members should be on roughly the same level of accomplishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller groups may lack differing opinions; larger groups require more reading time. Wide disparities in commitment or technical familiarity can cause discomfort. Find the right bunch of people you can trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript circulation timing and length limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should go out to everybody at least a week before the meeting; groups should set and stick to a length limit (preferably a word limit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Late manuscripts won't be critiqued until the next time. Use a word limit not a page limit to prevent manipulation by fonts/margins. Online groups must decide whether critique is continuous when a ms. is posted or limited to a time window for fairness to members' schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading aloud: when and cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading aloud can be enjoyable but may hide flaws and go too fast for listeners to make useful notes; prose ultimately must explain itself on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In-person groups may read a few pages aloud for enjoyment, but for prose narrative silent, slow, thoughtful reading is preferred and considered the greatest honor. Reading aloud is standard operating procedure for poetry workshops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Everyone must read others' manuscripts carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone writes; everyone reads — careful reading of other members' work is as important as submitting your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careless reading, delay, and failure to read are forgivable only occasionally. Online groups must work out mechanisms for annotating; small nitpicks and queries are best written directly on the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nitpicks and small corrections belong on the manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Spelling, grammar corrections, and small queries are best written directly on the ms. which is returned to the author to study at leisure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online groups should agree on how to do this—one solution is for everyone to have the same editing software so notes can be shared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation: everyone critiques every piece
rubrics_metrics.description: Every person critiques every piece; in actual meetings each ms. is critiqued in turn and everyone (except the author) speaks in turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online, critiques may be read as they come in; in-person order is important. Free critique (no order) is possible only when group dynamics are well-established and no one habitually dominates or remains silent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique protocol: brevity, uninterrupted, focused, impersonal
rubrics_metrics.description: Each critique should be brief, without interruption, concerning important aspects of the piece, and impersonal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trivial quibbles should be written on the ms. The critic's knowledge of the author's character or intentions is irrelevant — discuss the writing, not the writer. Refer to 'the narrator' not 'you.' Avoid sneers, put-downs, or flame-throwing. If necessary, the group should time-limit each critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arguing with other critiquers; enlarge without repeating
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid challenging other critiquers; don't repeat points—enlarge the group discussion by adding new angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you agree with another's comment say so; if you disagree, explain how and why without animosity. The aim is constructive interchange, not argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: First impressions and naive reactions are useful
rubrics_metrics.description: First impressions, reactions from a first reading, even misunderstandings, can be extremely useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors often rely on first impressions; say naive reactions or questions without animosity and with the intent to improve the ms. Avoid phrasing that blames the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative criticism must indicate possibility of revision and include positives
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism tends to focus on what's wrong; to be useful, negative criticism should indicate ways to revise and also tell the writer what works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out where you were confused, surprised, annoyed, or delighted, and identify parts you like best. Savage dismissals of a piece's worth are unhelpful and harmful in a workshop context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the author, limit questions to direct factual yes/no with consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Address the author rather than other group members. You may ask the author only a direct, factual, yes-or-no question and only if you tell the group your question first and get their consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reason is that others may prefer to judge the text without author explanation. Never ask a question that requires a long explanation or defense. If the text doesn't answer the question, the most useful action may be to mark the problem for revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer suggestions respectfully; respect authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions for fixes may be valuable but should be offered respectfully; the story belongs to its author, not to the critic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if you are certain how to change something, phrase it as a suggestion. Avoid imposing your solution; leave the final decision with the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not say what the story reminds you of in other literature or movies
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid telling the author that their story reminds you of other works; respect the text as itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons can mislead or constrain the author. Focus criticism on the text's own aims and execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider what the story is about and how it fulfils itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the story by considering what it tries to do and how successfully it achieves those ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques should assess purpose, fulfillment, and possible ways the piece might achieve its ends better; focus on constructive avenues for revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit long-winded critiques; enforce time/word limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If members tend to give overly long critiques, the group should limit each critique to a few minutes (in-person) or set word limits (virtual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A group that tolerates egocentric, tiresome critiquing probably won't stay together. Intensity and interplay are essential; enforce limits to maintain dynamics and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of Silence for the author being critiqued
rubrics_metrics.description: Before and during the entire session, the author of the story under discussion is silent and offers no preliminary explanations or excuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If asked to answer a question, be sure the whole group consents and be as brief as possible. While being critiqued, make notes of comments and note recurring points. When discussion is over the author may speak briefly (ask outstanding questions) and should thank the critics. Silence prevents defensive responses and allows the author to hear how readers experience the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online-specific: don't reply to critique during exchange; read and reflect
rubrics_metrics.description: When working online, keep the Rule of Silence and do not reply to critique while discussion is ongoing; allow critiquers to reply to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author's job is to read the interchange, think, make notes, and only speak at the end if desired. This allows the critics' comments to develop and deepen without the author's defense.
